issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'Survival guilt' is hard to reconcile with a stalking trauma in the absence of any indication that other people died or were put at comparable lethal risk. For this trauma type, that appraisal is clinically implausible rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: A specific taste trigger is not impossible, but for stalking it lacks support from the rest of the profile: there are no memory items or contextual details suggesting an event involving gustatory cues. Given the formulation also has no Triggers ↔ Memory linkage, this trigger is clinically unsupported and difficult to explain in this profile.

vignette:
Callum Reeves is a 32-year-old married man of British descent who works as a private tutor in the suburbs of Portland, Oregon. He presented for assessment reporting a PCL-5 score of 59, describing a constellation of symptoms that had been building steadily over the eighteen months since he was stalked by a former tutoring client - a situation that began as unsettling and escalated, over several months, into something that left him fundamentally altered in how he understood the world and his place within it.

The stalking began gradually. A parent of one of Callum's students started appearing at locations he hadn't mentioned - outside the coffee shop where he prepared lesson plans, in the parking lot of his gym, eventually idling on his residential street on a motorcycle, the engine cutting out just as Callum reached his front door. The man never made overt threats; he simply watched. When Callum reported the behaviour, the response from authorities was slow and the legal process inconclusive. The stalker's demeanour throughout - eerily calm, almost pleasant - meant that Callum began to doubt his own perception of danger. By the time a restraining order was finally issued, the damage was done. What frightened Callum most, in retrospect, was not any single incident but the realisation that someone could study him, know his patterns, and present an ordinary face to the world while doing so.

That realisation reshaped how Callum read other people entirely. He had come to believe that people are not what they seem - that the surface presentation of a person reveals nothing reliable about their intentions. When, in his tutoring sessions, a parent raises their voice even slightly, or expresses frustration in what anyone else might consider a measured tone, Callum finds himself scanning for threat: the tightened jaw, the shift in posture, the controlled anger that he now reads as a precursor to something worse. These moments of perceived anger, however ordinary, pull him back into the logic of the stalking - reinforcing his conviction that people cannot be trusted and that he himself cannot reliably judge who is safe. The cycle feeds itself: the more his appraisals of others darken, the more triggers he finds in ordinary social exchanges, and the more ordinary social exchanges become potential triggers.

Callum works from home most days, and the suburban streets outside his window have become a landscape of threat. The sound of a motorcycle engine - common enough in his neighbourhood - reliably produces a jolt of alarm that he describes as indistinguishable from the feeling of being watched. He avoids unfamiliar locations because, as he puts it, he cannot assess the danger when he doesn't know the exits, the sightlines, the patterns of movement. This hypervigilance keeps him in a state of chronic readiness that makes sleep nearly impossible; he lies awake cataloguing sounds, and the exhaustion that follows further erodes his capacity to distinguish genuine threat from false alarm. He frequently reacts as though he is in danger when nothing is actually wrong - a response he recognises intellectually but cannot override.

The strategies Callum has adopted to manage this state have, over time, made it worse. He avoids relaxing deliberately, having concluded that lowering his guard is what allowed the stalking to take hold in the first place. This refusal to rest sustains a baseline of physiological arousal that keeps him primed to detect threat in stimuli that would otherwise pass unnoticed. He has also pulled back emotionally from his wife, Nadia, telling himself that closeness is a vulnerability he can no longer afford - that people cannot be trusted, and this extends, in his darker moments, even to her. Most troublingly, he has developed a pattern of punitive self-talk, telling himself that he deserves to suffer for having failed to recognise the danger sooner. This belief - that his own judgment is fundamentally untrustworthy - compounds his distrust of others and leaves him caught between suspicion of the world and contempt for himself.

What finally brought Callum to seek help was a session with a fifteen-year-old student whose father arrived early and waited in the hallway. Callum heard footsteps pacing and spent the remainder of the hour unable to teach. He cancelled the following week's sessions and told Nadia he thought he was losing his mind. He came to the intake appointment hoping, cautiously, that something could be recovered - though he was not certain he deserved it.
